problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s$, where the curve $C$ is given in polar form by $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$
worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2}\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =4{cos}^{4}⁡\theta \cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =8{cos}^{5}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}8{cos}^{5}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{cos}^{5}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}16{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{cos}^{5}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =16{\int }_{1}^{1/2}-{u}^{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-16\cdot \frac{1}{6}{u}^{6}{|}_{1}^{1/2} \\  & =-\frac{16}{6}({(\frac{1}{2})}^{6}-{1}^{6}) \\  & =-\frac{8}{3}(-\frac{63}{64}) \\  & =\frac{21}{8}\end{aligned}
$$
